strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of multimodal misinformation benchmarks: misleading narratives can remain superficially consistent across images and captions. Specifying desired influence and execution plans before generation provides a useful framework for controlled investigation.

The benchmark contains 12,000 examples across ten news topics, with reference articles, two manipulation severities, and separate textual and visual modifications. Generating non-misleading variants also helps avoid equating synthetic content with misinformation.
The evaluation covers 14 VLMs and includes informative comparisons of prompting strategies, input modalities, caption styles, authenticity hints, and image generators.

Human verification provides encouraging initial evidence for binary-label quality, particularly for text, where agreement with dataset labels reaches 99.2% and inter-annotator agreement is substantial.
weaknesses: The central construct of creator intent is insufficiently validated. Knowing the generation instruction establishes intended synthetic provenance, but does not establish that this intent is expressed or recoverable from the resulting content. Tasks 1 and 2 largely measure inconsistency detection and manipulation localization; the benchmark lacks controls separating deliberate deception from accidental errors or legitimate framing. The broad societal-influence labels may also reflect news topics rather than identifiable communicative goals.

Human validation does not resolve this concern. Three annotators assess only binary misleadingness on 240 examples, using original-versus-generated pairs that provide information unavailable to evaluated models. Specific desire labels and manipulation severity are not validated. Agreement with image labels is only 89.2%, without an analysis or adjudication of the disagreements.

The tasks are coupled in ways that weaken the conclusions. Figures 9–10 require source and desire predictions only after a positive misinformation prediction, so low desire F1 includes upstream detection failures and cannot independently establish poor intent reasoning. Separate evaluation with the detection label supplied is needed. Near-universal non-misleading predictions from some models also warrant output-format and instruction-following audits before being attributed to reasoning limitations.

Despite broad model coverage, important baselines are absent: specialized evidence-based misinformation systems, simple entailment approaches, and topic-only baselines for desire prediction. A matched comparison against synthesis without explicit intent planning would help establish what the proposed construction contributes beyond existing manipulation benchmarks.

Real-world generalization remains unestablished. The dataset derives from 2,000 VisualNews stories using a GPT-4o-controlled synthesis pipeline, and evaluation supplies a trustworthy reference article. There is no naturally occurring misinformation evaluation. Substantial improvements with GPT-image-1 in Table 6 also suggest that visual generation fidelity and perception contribute to the measured difficulty; these factors are not separated from intent reasoning.

The shortcut analyses support sensitivity more strongly than their proposed explanations. The style experiment lacks non-misleading controls and verification that rewriting preserves factual meaning. Authenticity hints explicitly assert reliability or unreliability, so performance changes can reflect responses to supplied instructions or priors. These experiments do not isolate the claimed underlying reasoning mechanisms.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the supplied evaluation prompts and model identifiers. F1 averaging, response parsing, invalid-output handling, and generation settings are unspecified; data and code access are promised without an accessible artifact identified in the manuscript. Table 3 reports only nine of the fourteen models without explanation, and the Qwen 7B model identity differs between Tables 2 and 7.

Several analyses support narrower conclusions than claimed. The analyses do not adequately isolate the mechanisms claimed. Controls separating factual inconsistency, accidental error, and deliberate misleadingness are needed to establish the contribution beyond existing manipulation and fact-checking benchmarks.

Human verification does not establish that the intended labels are recoverable from the model’s inputs. Annotators compare original and modified content, whereas models receive the modified content and reference article; intent-alignment judgments additionally reveal the intended desire or plan. These checks assess compatibility rather than independent intent inference. Image-label agreement is only 89.2%, and image desire alignment is 86.3%, leaving meaningful ambiguity that is not analyzed by category or severity.

The comparisons do not isolate the value of intent-guided construction. There are no specialized misinformation-detection baselines, comprehensive unimodal controls, or topic-based baselines for desire prediction. The transfer experiment compares fine-tuning only against untuned models and uses binary labels rather than intent supervision. Matched-data and matched-compute training controls are necessary to attribute gains specifically to the proposed approach.

The task formulation confounds desire inference with upstream detection. The prompts require an NA response for desire whenever the model predicts non-misleading, so low desire F1 can arise from detection failures rather than an independent inability to infer communicative goals. Conditional or oracle-detection evaluations are missing. F1 averaging and invalid-output handling are also unspecified, which matters given the all-non-misleading predictions and near-zero scores of several models.

Some diagnostic experiments do not support their causal interpretation. Table 9’s purportedly style-only rewrites introduce additional assertions, such as an explosion sparking outrage and demands for accountability. The modality and style analyses also omit non-misleading performance, making changes in discrimination difficult to separate from shifts in prediction bias. Authenticity hints demonstrate prompt sensitivity but do not by themselves establish reliance on superficial content cues.

Reproducibility and external validity remain limited. Generation prompts are deliberately withheld, dataset and code access are promised rather than provided, and generation settings and uncertainty estimates are incomplete. Most conclusions concern synthetic examples from one text generator and one primary image generator, with an authoritative reference article supplied. The small alternative-generator study and single binary-detection transfer benchmark do not sufficiently substantiate the broader claims about real-world creator-intent detection.

strengths: The benchmark provides 12,000 instances grounded in 2,000 reference articles, with text/image manipulations, two severity levels, and non-misleading synthetic controls. This offers a useful controlled testbed.
Evaluation spans 14 VLMs and includes modality ablations, stylistic reframing, authenticity hints, and an alternative image generator, providing substantial empirical coverage.
Three-annotator validation examines label correctness, realism, and intent alignment. Reported label agreement is particularly strong for text: 99.2% accuracy and Fleiss’ kappa of 0.877.
Transfer results are promising: fine-tuning improves MMFakeBench macro-F1 by 7.96 points for LLaVA and 30.70 points for Qwen, suggesting potential training-data utility.
weaknesses: The central distinction between creator-intent reasoning and factual inconsistency detection is insufficiently established. Malicious generation instructions produce distortions, while benign instructions preserve the reference context. This construction confounds intent with content inconsistency; accidental-error controls and factual-consistency baselines are needed to demonstrate the claimed distinction.

Creator desire inference is not evaluated independently. Figures 9–10 require models to output NA whenever detection predicts non-misleading, so low desire F1 partly reflects upstream detection failures. Evaluation with known misleading labels, an explicit F1 aggregation definition, and article-only/topic baselines would clarify whether models actually struggle to infer desires beyond recognizing the news domain.

The comparisons do not establish the added value of intent-guided construction. Specialized misinformation detectors and matched synthetic-data baselines are absent. The transfer experiment uses only binary supervision, two small models, and one external validation set; its gains could reflect ordinary task fine-tuning rather than benefits specific to modeling creator intent.

Human validation supports plausibility more strongly than recoverability of intent. Annotators see original/generated pairs, and intent-alignment judgments reveal the intended labels rather than require independent inference. The 240-instance audit also finds 10.8% disagreement with image labels, without subsequent correction or severity-specific analysis. Direct evidence for real-world creator-intent inference remains missing.

Several diagnostic interpretations lack adequate controls. Stylistic rewrites are not independently checked for semantic preservation; Table 9 introduces claims such as public outrage and demands for accountability. Likewise, changing image generators can change manipulation strength and instruction adherence alongside visual fidelity. These experiments do not cleanly isolate the proposed causes.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful evaluation prompts and model identifiers. Generation prompts are withheld, dataset access is only promised, and output-parsing/error handling is unspecified. The complete all-negative collapse of some models warrants explicit implementation and prompt-format checks before being interpreted as an intent-reasoning limitation.

strengths: DECEPTIONDECODED provides a substantial, structured resource: 12,000 variants from 2,000 news items across ten topics, covering both modalities, manipulation severities, and non-misleading controls.
Evaluation across 14 VLMs, two prompting approaches, modality ablations, stylistic changes, and authenticity hints provides useful evidence of model sensitivity.
Human validation covers label correctness, plausibility, and alignment with generation objectives. Reported binary-label agreement is strong for text (99.2%) and reasonably high for images (89.2%).
Transfer experiments provide preliminary evidence of practical utility: fine-tuning improves MMFakeBench macro-F1 by 7.96 and 30.70 points for two models.
weaknesses: The central construct is insufficiently validated. Misleading examples deliberately depart from a reference article, while benign examples preserve it; consequently, intent is confounded with factual inconsistency. Figure 10 explicitly operationalizes intent through inconsistency. Controls involving accidental inaccuracies and misleading but factually accurate framing, together with established fact-checking baselines, are needed to demonstrate a distinct intent-reasoning contribution.

Human validation does not establish that the intended desires are recoverable from the model inputs. Annotators see original–modified pairs and, in Appendix E.3, the proposed desire or execution plan. Agreement therefore establishes compatibility with a supplied interpretation, rather than independent recovery among plausible alternatives. The 89.2% image-label agreement also leaves meaningful label uncertainty without a reported adjudication procedure.

The evaluation does not adequately separate reasoning failures from prediction and instruction-following biases. Two models always predict non-misleading in Table 2, yielding 33.3% binary accuracy, while an always-misleading baseline would achieve 66.7%. Output-format diagnostics and calibrated baselines are missing. Moreover, desire prediction is conditioned on positive detection, so its F1 conflates detection errors with desire-inference errors.

The transfer experiment compares binary fine-tuning only against untuned models. Without matched training on existing misinformation data or intent-agnostic synthetic data, the gains cannot establish the specific benefit of intent-guided construction. Training uses no explicit desire supervision, and potential source-event overlap with MMFakeBench is not audited.

Some robustness conclusions exceed the controls. Style rewriting is tested only on misleading captions, without verified semantic preservation; Table 9 changes 'raises questions' to 'sparks outrage,' introducing a different claim. The generator comparison likewise uses only misleading images and changes manipulation visibility alongside fidelity. These experiments demonstrate sensitivity more convincingly than they isolate failures of intent reasoning.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a benchmark contribution. Generation prompts are withheld, no dataset or code access link is supplied, F1 averaging and output parsing are unspecified, and uncertainty estimates are absent. The documented model versions, evaluation prompts, and fine-tuning settings help, but do not resolve these gaps.
